sections.text: Please tell me all about Thy glorious manifestations, by means of which Thou pervadest the world.
O Master! How shall I, by constant meditation, know Thee? My Lord! What are Thy various manifestations through which I am to mediate on Thee?
Tell me again, I pray, about the fullness of Thy power and Thy glory; for I feel that I am never satisfied when I listen to Thy immortal words.

We had been discussing chapter 10, Vibhuti yoga, Yoga of divine Glory. In the first six chapters. Chapter two gave us the real indicator of who we are.
The paradigm shift in chapter two was you are not the mortal being, but you are the immortal being having mortal equipment. As long as you identify with your mortal equipment, you are mortal. But if you identify with immortal being, you are immortal.
The quest of my life is to exist, and therefore the only remedy is to identify with the immortal being, not with the mortal equipment. The remaining segment of the first six chapters dealt with actions, because actions are the unit of my interface with this world. So the first six chapters give us the pluralistic view of the world and myself.
The segment ended with Dhyana yoga, Yoga of Contemplation, meditation. How do I now change my worldview from pluralistic to singularistic? The technique is meditation, but then what to meditate upon will be the next six chapters, 7 to 12, which is that Tat aspect of Tattvamasi. There are four Mahavakyas we have seen before in the Upanishads.
One is Prajnanam Brahma , Consciousness is brahman. Thats the very first. The next is Ayam Atma Brahma.
So if consciousness is Brahman, then my Atma is Brahman , my consciousness is Brahman. The next one says Tattvamasi , That thou art, that which you are seeking as immortal existence is you, is your own self. And the last one is Aham Brahmasmi.
Once that realization takes place, its Oh, I am that consciousness. The Gita is an elaboration on the third, which is Tattvamasi. So the Tat , that which I consider right now something other than me, Bhagavan is somebody other than me. I know all my limitations, all my papas and punyas.
Bhagavan has none of those. So hes something other than me. That is described in chapters 7 to 12.
The seventh chapter was Jnana Vijnana Yoga , Yoga of Knowledge and its application. Vijnana is Vishishta Jnana, applied knowledge. When its applied, it becomes Vijnana.
So in Jnana Vijnana Yoga we got a glimpse of reality , that there are two ways to look at it. One is the pluralistic view, the other the singularistic view. When we look at the pluralistic, its called Prakriti, the world of the manifested universe.
As we know, where I exist, he exists, it exists, and everything else exists. Thats the world of Prakriti. But that is my lower Prakriti, because you can perceive, feel, and experience it through your senses.
Therefore its the lower Prakriti. Other than that is my higher Prakriti, which is unmanifested. The higher Prakriti cannot be perceived through your senses.
So he said, there are two Prakritis. The source of all the beings and things in this world are these two Prakritis , these two natures, higher and lower. Whether you look at it from a singularistic way or a pluralistic way.
That was chapter seven. Chapter eight was Imperishable Brahman. How do I recognize that imperishable Brahman, that which is the source of all beings? He says, Aham Kṛtsnasya Jagadaha , I am the source of all the things and beings.
How do I recognize that the self is imperishable? That is given in chapter 8. Chapter 9 was Rajavidya Rajaguhya Yoga, the Yoga of the Royal Secret. The secret is the relationship , the relation-less relationship I have with that source.
Bhagavan said, I am not in them, but they are in me. All the things and beings which we perceive, feel, touch, interact, and react with in this world , Bhagawan said, they are in me, I am not in them. Which is totally contrary to what we have heard all our life from our childhood.
Bhagavan is in every being. Bhagavan is in your heart, my heart, his heart. Bhagawan says, no, I am not anywhere.
They are all in me, but I am not in them. He also turned around and said, but they are also not in me. So it is something for us to contemplate.
How can that relationship exist where he is not in me, but I am in him, but I am also not in him? So the analogy we had used before to understand this: space in a car. Is the space in the car, or is the car in the space? BMW or Mercedes , is the space in the car, or is the car in the space? We clearly know space is in the car. We have already four people. We dont have space in my car. But if thats the case, what happened to the space which was in the car when it was manufactured in Germany and sealed tight and transported to United States? What happened to the German space? Did I bring it with me or we left it in Germany? Well, the answer is obviously we didnt import space, we only imported the car.
So car must be in this space. Space cannot be in the car. Car moved in the space.
And now if you consider that this space and the car are made up of the same entity called nothingness, then space can say, car is not in me. See, we have difficulty understanding this because we think this is solid world of matter and the space is no matter. But scientists have been trying to find a solid matter in this world and they have not been successful so far.
First we thought that you need a matter atom. Then we found out atom is nothing but a hole of space. Theres nothing in it other than electrons and protons.
The nucleus must be a solid material. They found out thats not solid either. We are yet to find any solid material anywhere in this universe.
So if you consider that both the car and the space are made up of the same material, then space can say, Car is not in me. So Bhagavan said, I am not in them, they are in me. The beings as they perceive, they are in my own self. They are there because of me.
If I am not there, they are not there. But they are also not there. Because I have never changed into these beings.
Therefore they are also not in me. Thats my relation-less relationship with my Lord. How do I recognize it? As we discussed in chapter nine.
But now Im more confused. Arjuna said, What do I contemplate? I cannot contemplate on nothingness. As I said, in architecture, the first exercise was how to perceive space. So if you take space and remove everything out of this space, you cannot perceive space, only perceive space in the relationship of objects.
There are two objects in architecture. We used to say we created three spaces. Two positive space and one negative space in between.
And thats how you now perceive positive, negative, positive. Remove the positive, and the negative goes away. There is nothing to perceive.
So this is my dilemma. People are telling me Bhagavan is everywhere, Bhagavan is everything. But how do I relate to him? So chapter 10 is Vibhuti Yoga, Yoga of the Divine Glories.
How do I see the divine glories in my world of plurality and contemplate on the singularity? That is chapter 10. In the beginning of the chapter, Bhagawan said, do not try with your intellect or your senses. Na Me Vidhuh Sura Ganaha , even the Devas do not know me, nor the Rishis.
The Devas are our Indriyas. That which is illuminating this world for me is my Devas. This world is illuminated by my senses , my world of sight, my world of sound, my world of touch.
With that capability, I cannot be known. Nor can the Maha Rishis know me. By Rishis is meant my intellect , by my thought process of inferring knowledge, even thats not possible.
The intellect is not capable. My senses are not capable. So Bhagavan said, I will tell you how you should contemplate on me.
He said, Aham Sarvasya Prabhava, Mattaha Sarva Pravartate , start thinking first that I pervade everywhere, I am the source of all being. And Mattaha Sarva Pravartate, Iti Matva Bhajante Mam Budhaha Bhava Samanvitaha. Thus, whoever contemplates on me is a wise person, one endowed with loving consciousness.
He will start with this very notion that he is the source of all being. We will have great difficulty if the president of our country is not to our liking and we are told he is also Krishnas manifestation. Bhagawan said, you have to overcome that.
If you dont overcome that, you have failed at the starting line. You have to overcome that. Iti Matva Bhajante Mam Priti Purvakam Bhava Samanvitaha.
With a loving consciousness , right now I divide my world into the world I love and the world I hate. Bhagawan says, if you want to know me, this world cannot be divided, because its only me. I cannot hate part of me.
I cannot love my right leg and hate my left leg. My left leg is as important as the right one, even though its broken. They say, if I develop that sense, then only will you be able to know me.
So Bhagawan gave that thumbnail sketch of how people can come to Macchittaha Madgat Pranaha Bodhayantaha Parasparam. You try to do it by yourself , you may be motivated for a few days. After that you will recede into what you were doing before.
Therefore, it is very important to have Bodhayantaha Parasparam , reinforce this idea in each other. Satsanga, the glory of Satsanga. This cannot be done by yourself.
Gita cannot be read in one sitting. You cant sit down and say, I learned Gita. When used to come, people would say, , we have gone through the Gita. used to say, Has the Gita gone through you? So it is very essential that we keep up our enthusiasm about knowing Bhagawan. We are very easy to drop off.
Somebody once said, I finally understood the difference between two worldviews. He said the basic difference is that one group starts with saying that human beings are basically bad, and you have to improve them. Their goal is: they start out bad, you have to improve them. The other group says human beings are basically good; they are victims of situations, and we have to help them.
Thats the big difference in worldview. So theyre very similar to what we say about the Hindu view and certain other religious views. Some religions start with the premise that the human being is a sinner who must be redeemed.
Hinduism says the human being is an immortal, divine being, and you have to purify him if there is impurity on him. So Bhagavan here says, whether you start from evil or good, there is a very good possibility of impurities superimposing on you and dampening your enthusiasm. The only way you can make sure is Parasparam Bodhayantaha , because we see our world through others eyes.
If others approve what you are doing, we feel good about it. No matter how sure I am that I am doing good, if others dont approve, I wont feel good about it. Two people were working in a warehouse, painting the high trusses.
They are lazily leaning against each other, painting. One fell down, so other also fell down. Luckily they fell in a heap of garbage, so they were not hurt.
They got up, looked at each other. Ones face was completely dirtied, others was miraculously clean. The guy whose face was clean, he went to the bathroom, washed his face, then went to work.
The guy whose face was dirty, he didnt bother, he went straight to work. That was the question. The answer was, they looked at each other.
The guy said, his face is clean, mine must be clean too. Let me go and start working. The other guy said, his face is dirty, mine must be dirty too.

Arjunas request here is deeply practical: Tell me Your divine manifestations (Vibhutayah) by which You pervade these worlds. He understands the teaching intellectually but needs concrete pointers for meditation. His question Katham vidyam aham - How shall I know You? - acknowledges that knowing about God is different from experiencing Gods presence. The formless is difficult to contemplate; the mind needs hooks, anchors, tangible reference points. This is not spiritual weakness but honest acknowledgment of how human consciousness works.
Most striking is Arjunas declaration: Truptir hi shrinvato nasti me amritam - I am never satiated listening to Your nectar-like words. This insatiable thirst for spiritual knowledge marks the true seeker. Unlike ordinary desires that diminish with fulfillment, spiritual hunger grows the more it is fed. Each insight creates capacity for deeper insight; each experience of truth creates longing for more. This is the nature of approaching the infinite - there is always more.
Today, practice Arjunas approach: bring your honest questions to your spiritual practice. What specific pointers would help you recognize the divine in your daily experience? Notice whether your engagement with spiritual teachings feels like obligation or genuine thirst. If the fire seems dim, perhaps you need fresh fuel - new questions, new perspectives, renewed wonder. Ask yourself: Am I approaching spirituality as a subject to master or a mystery to explore? What would it take to feel genuine, insatiable curiosity about the nature of reality?
